name: Metta (loving-kindness) and jhana (absorption) meditation
origin: Both come from early Buddhist teachings of ancient India, preserved in the Pali texts and in later commentaries such as the 5th century Visuddhimagga, and in recent decades teachers such as Ayya Khema and Leigh Brasington have taught them to lay students, many of them in the West.
summary: Metta is the deliberate cultivation of goodwill: silently wishing yourself and others well until a warm, friendly feeling fills the mind. Jhanas are a series of deeply absorbed states of attention, traditionally eight, marked first by joy and pleasure that fill the body and then by deep calm and even-mindedness (equanimity). This point covers loving-kindness practice, metta taken all the way into absorption, and jhana practice in general.
theoryOfChange: Repeatedly generating goodwill is thought to build positive emotions and a felt sense of connection, which may soften self-criticism and hostility. Taking that warm feeling into absorption trains very steady attention and gives direct access to calm, non-sensual pleasure; Buddhist texts describe jhana as setting aside sensual desire and other hindrances, and as a tool for developing insight. A brain imaging study of one meditator with about 6,000 hours of practice linked the extreme joy of jhana to the brain's dopamine and opioid reward system, which fits the idea that the pleasure is generated from within.
whatYouDo: Sitting quietly, you bring someone to mind and silently repeat phrases such as 'may you be happy' or 'may you be free from suffering', moving from yourself to loved ones, neutral people, difficult people and finally all beings. For jhana, attention is first steadied, often on the breath (called access concentration); you then rest attention on a pleasant, warm feeling itself, such as the glow of metta, and let it grow without grasping until attention becomes absorbed. Deeper jhanas are usually learned on retreats with many hours of sitting a day and guidance from a teacher.
typicalDose: Loving-kindness: studied as self-guided practice and as courses lasting from a few days to about 12 weeks, and one meta-analysis found that course length and practice time did not change the size of the benefit. Jhana: usually learned on retreats with many hours of sitting a day, then kept up with daily practice; the expert meditators in the brain studies had about 17 and more than 25 years of practice.
keyTechniques: Goodwill phrases such as 'may you be happy'
Widening circle: self, loved ones, neutral and difficult people, all beings
Resting on the pleasant feeling and letting it grow
Moving through the jhanas from joy toward calm and equanimity
Related heart practices: compassion, shared joy, equanimity

evidence.summary: Loving-kindness is fairly well studied: a meta-analysis (a pooled analysis) of 24 studies with 1,759 people found that it increases positive emotions, with medium effects for programs focused on loving-kindness and small effects for those focused on compassion (Zeng and colleagues, 2015). An earlier review of 22 randomized trials concluded that it 'facilitates positive emotions, although they are not entirely consistent', and warned that small trials made its estimates imprecise (Galante and colleagues, 2014). No controlled trials of jhana were found: the evidence is brain imaging of single expert meditators (Hagerty and colleagues, 2013; Yang, Sacchet and colleagues, 2024), which shows the states are distinct and can be entered at will, not that they improve mental health, so the moderate rating reflects the loving-kindness research rather than jhana.

goodFitFor: People who want more warmth, kindness and positive emotion in daily life, and practitioners with a steady sitting habit who want deep calm and concentration.
cautions: Wishing yourself well can stir up grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, especially after trauma or with strong self-criticism, so starting with someone easy to love and keeping sessions short can help. Intensive jhana practice can bring strong energy, body sensations or altered states, and some people start chasing the pleasant states; it is best learned with an experienced teacher, and anyone with a history of psychosis, mania or dissociation should talk to a clinician first.
namingNote: Often written 'meta', the Pali word is metta (Sanskrit maitri), meaning goodwill or loving-kindness. In this map metta and jhana form one point: loving-kindness practice, metta developed until it becomes absorbing (the brahmavihara or 'divine abiding' jhanas), and jhana practice in general, whatever the starting object. Teachers disagree on how deep jhana must be, from lighter 'sutta-oriented' states to the very deep absorption described in the Visuddhimagga, and Sparby and Sacchet (2024) distinguish three types; this point covers the whole range. It is kept apart from Vipassana, which investigates change in experience rather than building absorption, and from Do Nothing, which has no object at all.
